title: Neither do I condemn thee (John 8:1–11)
hookLine: the crowd has stones, he writes in the dust, and they leave one by one
last: TODAY SALVATION CAME TO THIS HOUSE.

lines: A WOMAN DRAGGED INTO THE CROWD.
cards: Early morning in the Temple courts. Jesus is sitting, teaching a crowd. Suddenly, a commotion.

Some scribes and Pharisees push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone. She's been caught, they say, in the act of adultery. Moses in the Law, they say, commanded such a one to be stoned.
So what do you say? John tells us plainly it's a trap. If he says let her go, he's set aside the Law.
If he says stone her, where's the mercy he's known for? Everyone waits. There are stones within reach.

teach.h: WHAT DID HE WRITE? JOHN DOESN'T SAY.
teach.b: What did he write? The Gospel never says. People have guessed ever since; some early Christian writers imagined he wrote the accusers' own sins in the dirt.
But John leaves it blank, and it's honest to leave it blank too. They keep pressing him.

teach.h: LET HIM WITHOUT SIN CAST FIRST.
teach.b: So he straightens up and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't stare them down.

teach.h: ONE BY ONE, THE ELDEST FIRST.
teach.b: One by one they go away, John says, beginning with the eldest. Maybe they had the most to remember. Until it's just Jesus and the woman, still standing there.
And where is the man? The Law they cite names both the man and the woman. The text is silent about him.
Then Jesus looks up and speaks to her, maybe the first person all morning to speak to her rather than about her. Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?
No one, Lord. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Neither will I condemn thee. Go, and now sin no more."

teach.h: NO CONDEMNING, AND A NEW LIFE.
teach.b: Both halves matter: no condemnation, and a new life.

teach.h: GO, AND NOW SIN NO MORE.
teach.b: He doesn't pretend nothing happened, and he doesn't throw a stone. The Catholic Church receives this passage as sacred Scripture, part of John's Gospel, and reads it at Mass in Lent.

how: Catholics hear this Gospel on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year C, and it is often preached before confession as a picture of mercy that frees a person and sends them into a new life.

games.q: you're holding a stone. the teacher has just said: let the one without sin throw first. what do the accusers do?
o: they leave one by one, beginning with the eldest.
they argue with him about the Law.
games.why: they go away one by one, the eldest first. then: “Neither will I condemn thee. Go, and now sin no more.”

practice: Is there someone you've been holding a stone for, someone whose mistake you keep replaying, maybe someone the whole group is talking about?
Picture the stone in your hand and feel its weight; you don't have to decide what they did was fine, just open your hand and set it down in the dust.
Then, if you want, turn the same mercy toward yourself, and if you pray, hear his words spoken to you.

wordCard.voice: condemn. What Jesus would not do to the woman the crowd wanted to stone, before telling her to sin no more.

orig.note: Greek: to condemn, to judge against. The word Jesus uses to the woman: neither do I condemn you.

carryVoice: Your line: go, and sin no more. Mercy first, then a new start. Day fifty-five, done.
